Generally it's putting systems under their max (and sometimes above the max stated in documentation) load to see how long they stay up, and where problems arise (disk read/write speed, buffer space, etc...). In my case I'm doing a lower rate (~25% of max) and running for extended periods, usually for several months. Change the algorithm. Why is the front page of /r/all full of 10 minute old posts with 2 upvotes?

I've mentioned this before but reddit's rank system, which I assume voat copied, is actually time based. The voting manipulates the post's timestamp, essentially up votes move the post forward in time and seem newer, improving is rank. The vote total parameter is logarithmic though, so 1 positive had the same effect as the next 9, and as the next 90 after that and so on. This is so no matter how many up votes a post gets, it will eventually drop off in the ranking as the voting can't cancel the time elapsed anymore.

EDIT: see this post. Looks like it's because the rank only gets updated when someone votes on it, or probably a combination of this and what I said above.

It looks like the algorithm hasn't been tweaked to account for the much lower traffic here, and the time element of the ranking dominates the vote total element. As a result, with the exception of the few really popular posts, everything else with votes in the single digits are all basically just ranked by newness.

You assume wrong. Voat’s ranking is based on HackerNews, not Reddit. Also, voting does not “manipulate the post’s timestamp” on either Reddit or Voat, although you are right in that there is a logarithmic factor.

Here is Voat’s relatively simple ranking code.

The Reddit code is somewhat more complex, with more ranking options, but here’s the relevant “hot” algo.

Thanks for the correction and details on the Voat system, I've always found this stuff interesting. Still, I think my original point still stands overall. Fundamentally, voat's ranking system is still a function of both time and vote total, and the coefficients (the 0.8 and 1.8 exponents in this case, I think) need to be tweaked so to reflect a smaller community voting on posts so that the time variable in the function doesn't swamp out the vote variable, leaving /v/all always ranked basically by new.

As far as the "manipulate timestamp" thing, no you're right they don't literally change the timestamp, but conceptually it's accurate since the log(score) term is added directly to the time. In other words, the score gets converted to units of time and that's what ultimately the ranking variable is in units of too. This article explains it pretty well in detail.

Btw, sorry for being brusque in the previous comment. I just dislike assumptions when information is readily available :)

The ranking definitely could use improvement but it’s a complex problem with a constantly shifting target (growing userbase, increasing rate of submissions). If you can come up with specific changes to the formula and substantiate the improvement I might suggest you open an issue on Github to talk about it. Atko seems quite fond of the HackerNews-style ranking but developers are (usually) not good economists ;)
Here's why it happens. It does need to be fixed (shameless plug to a relevant ideasforvoat submission).

The timestamp thing it a good idea, that's actually how reddit does it. Each post gets a timestamp referenced to some common, arbitrary date. The time is assigned once and never needs to be updated and new posts just have bigger time stamps assigned, which out-ranks the older post's timestamp (vote counts being equal).

I've had this idea for a while now and I've actually been working on it a bit, but it's FAR from finished.
It's like a steampunky skyrim-esque open world RPG. The basic idea is that the world was hit by a meteor about a hundred years ago, and the meteor hit the Earth in the direction of its spin, causing it to no longer spin and just stand still (I know this probably wouldn't work irl, but it's just an idea), so one side of the Earth is uncomfortably hot, and the other side is a bit nippy. So, the only places society has been able to form is around the fringes of the hot and cold areas of the Earth.
Now, there's another angle to this as well. The Earth had always had monsters on it, but none of them could survive in the light, so they never really took hold on Earth due to its 12 hour darkness cycles. Well, know that half of the Earth is permanently dark, the monsters have kind of run amok and started growing in numbers. They're really becoming an issue for the people that live on the fringes.
Now, you play as a guy (who's name is yet to be determined) that lived with his family on the darker sides of the fringes, rather than smack in the center or closer to the hot side. Due to the location of him and his family, they occasionally had to fight off the beasts of the darkness. Well one day, they became overwhelmed and, as hard as he fought, the man couldn't fend off the fiends and they slaughtered his family. The only reason he was able to escape was because another man who lived in a cottage not far from them heard the gunshots and ran over to help. The man then decided to get retribution for his family and kill every monster he came across.
So that's kind of where I'm at right now. I'm thinking the world will be about the size of Skyrim and will probably borrow quite a few mechanics from it, but I want it to be a completely different thing from that. I'm not sure yet. I might even make it a sidescrolling open world RPG, kind of like Terraria. All I know is how I want the game to feel, what I want for a story, and that I want it to lean heavily on RPG mechanics.
For the basic feel of the game, it's going to be very steampunk, but very dark at the same time. This song (which actually gave me the inspiration for the game) might give you a bit of an insight as to what it would feel like.

At first glance, the game I've been dreaming of looks a lot like No Man's Sky or Rodina. It also takes a lot of inspiration from Escape Velocity: Nova and its predecessors. An online, freeform sci-fi epic with a huge galaxy to explore and plenty of ways to leave your mark on it.

I'm not so interested in walking around on alien worlds, interacting with wildlife, or navigating interiors. My game would be more focused on invention, customization, and commerce. Players would be able to customize, upgrade, and personalize every component of their ships (among other things) and construct bases and factories for unlocking specialized tech. The tech trees would be insanely deep and varied, unknown and influenced by a number of factors like research focus, funding, manpower, player skills, environmental conditions, and available materials, to encourage experimentation. No two player-controlled companies would be able to manufacture identical products. Players would be able to ramp up production and sell their tech to others, or leverage its uniqueness for their own gain.

You could dive as deeply into the business aspect of gameplay as you like, but there would be plenty for unentrepreneurial players to do too: Exploration and colonization, political and military action, piracy, smuggling, and plenty of interesting scripted plotlines to unravel.

An open world MMO based on the cartoon Reboot

It was a Canadian CG cartoon from the 90's that was way ahead of its time in terms of animation quality.

Basically, it was set inside of a computer. All the characters were called sprites and usually represented either programs or bits of code. The main character, a guardian named Bob, was anti virus software. The main bad guy was a virus named Megabyte.

In this computer world, the mysterious user would occasionally drop games into their environment. If the user won the game, it would destroy that sector and nullify any sprites caught in the game. It's was Bob's job to ensure the system always won the games. Eventually some of the characters got trapped in the web and had to travel from system to system by game hopping.

So basically, you'd get an open world with random game events dropping down. You could make the world persistent, so that if one system lost too many games, it would be destroyed. Random encounters with viruses, opposing factions and maybe become powerful enough to invade the user's world through mobile technology.

Even if you just made it so you had to play the games, the amount of game-types could be near unlimited.

I have no idea how you would make or program such a beast, but it would be amazing in my mind.

World war z meets the sims. You are a survivor in command of a band of survivors. You can issue commands to your fellow survivors but they have free will like a sim and how well they listen or whether they listen at all depends on how much they respect you as a leader and how loyal they are, etc. People would be your most valuable resource. Finding a survivor would be good for your group because there is safety in numbers but one bite on a non immune survivor would be the end of them and there are more ways to die than just that. Gunfights with other bands of survivors would need to be avoided at all costs because it could easily mean the end of your group. Injuries would be realistic. Gunshot wounds would most likely be fatal, but if its in a non vital area like a leg or shoulder and you have a survivor who is medically trained or good at first aid and your group can peotect this survivor for long enough, perhaps they could recover. Skills would make certain survivors more valuable too. Maybe some survivors are very physically fit and also immune to the virus making them an asset for clearing zombies with melee weapons...perhaps other survivors dont have such a tough constitution but before the outbreak they got a doctorate in engineering and just happen to excel at creating efficient weapons out of scrap parts that could be found. You as leader have to decide where best to put each individual based on their skills and abilities. Its probably not a great idea to have your only medically trained survivor on the front lines. This would be world war z style too so the numbers of zombies would be high enough that resource to kill ratio would come into play. A bullet for every zombie would be extremely difficult but maybe with a properly set up base you could manage bows or crossbows with enough arrows to get by. Melee would also be increadibly useful but your survivors would eventually get tired and need to retreat from the hundreds of thousands of zeds in each town. Of course camping at base would be a recipe for disaster. You would need to organise clearing or raiding parties to go through small towns nearby to get weapons, ammo, medical supplies, food, water, building supplies, gasoline, even new survivors to recruit. Clearing or raiding these towns would be long affairs requiring days of play time to get through. Your survivors would have to clear literally thousands of zombies to completely clear the towns. Exhaustion would be a real danger and your survivors would be constantly on the brink of mental breakdown due to stress, depression, trauma and fear. Every resource would need to be carefully managed to ensure the survival of the new colony you are building. Slowly you would build your base into a new city with high walls and new jobs including clearing zombies from the walls, building homes, building weapons, doing laundry, etc. Corpses would pile up as well. If enough zeds followed a raiding band back to base, their corpses could pile up high enough to let zeds over the walls to bite your less immune workers. This would be a threat when clearing towns as well. Holding up on a rooftop sounds like a great idea until several hours in when the zeds are just climbing the pile of corpses to get to your survivors who are all so exhausted they can barely move their arms to pick up a weapon or even aim a gun properly. And how will you even know of a survivor is immune until they report that they've been bitten. Do you risk a survivor of unknown immunity status on the front lines? A break in your line could spell the end for your group but you only have a couple of survivors who are willing to fight and you need all the combat units you can get...each survivor would progress as the game went on too. Some survivors would break and crack under the stress, others would thrive and grow stronger after every nattle on the e front lines, slowly turning into highly efficient zombie clearing machines. Some survivors would learn mew trades in your little city. Picking up engineering skills or medical skills from other survivors or even studying the subjects from books found on raids.

I coukd go on for hours but i think you get the idea. It would be sort of like the sims mixed with world war z mixed with xcom.
